title: Beyond "Why Didn't She Leave?": Understanding Domestic Violence as a Pattern of Control - NewsBreak
text:
By CrimeCentral ,
14 hours ago The first installment of Crime Central’s October series, Behind Closed Doors: Domestic Violence, Crime, and the Systems That Respond.
Before You Read Reader Advisory This article discusses domestic violence, coercive control, stalking, sexual violence, and the risks that can follow separation. It does not include graphic descriptions.
If you are experiencing abuse, you do not have to decide about leaving in order to ask for help. You can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline 24/7 at 800-799-SAFE (7233), or text START to 88788. More resources are listed later in this post.
When people hear that someone was abused by a partner, one question tends to come up first.
Why didn’t she leave?
It comes up in conversations among friends and family. It comes up in courtrooms and in news coverage. Survivors often ask it of themselves.
It also comes in other versions. Why did the victim stay? Why did they return? Why didn’t they call the police, tell their family, seek a protection order, or take the children and go?
Every version begins from the same assumption: that leaving was a clear, available path and the victim chose not to take it.
It is not a neutral question.
It treats an abusive relationship like an ordinary relationship that has become unhappy, rather than a system built to restrict another person’s choices. It places the survivor’s decisions under scrutiny while the abusive partner’s conduct fades into the background.
A better question is not, “Why didn’t the victim leave?”
It is, “What did the abusive person do to make leaving difficult, dangerous, or seemingly impossible?”
That language shift puts responsibility back on the person choosing to abuse. It also forces us to see domestic violence as more than an isolated assault. Physical violence may be part of the pattern, but the pattern can also include surveillance, humiliation, sexual coercion, financial restriction, threats, stalking, isolation, and the slow destruction of a victim’s independence.
Understanding that pattern is necessary before discussing any individual case. Without it, we risk judging victims by how we imagine we would respond, instead of examining the conditions under which they were forced to make decisions.
Domestic Violence Is More Than Physical Violence Many people still picture domestic violence as a single visible act: a punch, a bruise, a broken object, a 911 call.
Those incidents matter. But they do not always reveal the structure of the abuse.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention defines intimate partner violence broadly enough to include physical violence, sexual violence, stalking, and psychological aggression by a current or former partner. Its 2023–2024 National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey found that more than one in three women and more than one in six men in the United States had experienced contact sexual violence, physical violence, or stalking by an intimate partner during their lifetimes. Nearly one in three women and more than one in five men reported psychological aggression.
The survey also separately measured behaviors connected to coercive control and entrapment: monitoring a partner’s whereabouts, limiting access to money, isolating them from family or friends, making decisions for them, destroying valued belongings, and using threats of harm or suicide.
Viewed one at a time, those behaviors can look unrelated. Together, they can form a system of domination.
Sociologist and forensic social worker Evan Stark gave that system its most influential framework. His central argument was that many abusive relationships are not primarily about assault. They are about liberty—one person systematically taking away another person’s ability to make their own choices. Violence can be part of that pattern, but it is often the enforcement mechanism rather than the whole system.
In practice, an abusive partner may insist on knowing where the victim is at all times. They may demand passwords, track a phone, read messages, control transportation, interfere with work, or create conflict whenever the victim sees friends or relatives. They may place every account in their own name, hand out an allowance, and scrutinize every purchase. They may threaten to disclose private information, report an immigrant partner to authorities, take the children, harm a pet, ruin the victim’s reputation, or hurt themselves if the victim leaves.
Many of these behaviors may not constitute crimes on their own, which is one reason coercive control can be easy to overlook.
The harm is cumulative. Each tactic narrows the victim’s freedom a little more, until everyday decisions—where to go, whom to speak with, what to wear, whether to work, when to sleep, how to spend money—carry the possibility of punishment.
Not every unhealthy, selfish, or hurtful act is coercive control. The term describes a repeated pattern used to dominate, frighten, isolate, or entrap an intimate partner. Context matters: Who is afraid? Whose choices are being restricted? Who must constantly adjust their behavior to prevent retaliation? Who benefits from the pattern?
Some legal systems have begun to catch up. England and Wales created a specific offense of controlling or coercive behavior in 2015, and Scotland followed with a broader domestic abuse offense in 2018. In the United States, a handful of states have added coercive control to the definitions used in family and protective-order law, though criminal statutes remain rare.
The Invisible Work of Survival People living with abuse often become skilled at reading danger.
They learn what a change in tone means, a particular look, a car in the driveway, a silence that lasts too long. They know which subjects to avoid, when to move the children into another room, where to keep important documents, and how to make an ordinary explanation sound convincing.
From the outside, some of their choices can look passive or inconsistent. From inside the relationship, those choices may be deliberate attempts to reduce harm.
A victim may apologize for something they did not do because an apology ends the immediate threat. They may deny abuse in front of police because the abusive partner will still be there after the officers leave. They may recant, minimize, or refuse to cooperate with a prosecution because they fear retaliation, financial collapse, custody consequences, deportation, homelessness, or involvement from other systems. They may stay in contact after separation because they share children, housing, debt, a workplace, a community, or a court order requiring communication.
None of these actions prove that the abuse did not happen.
The U.S. Department of Justice has cautioned prosecutors that people affected by domestic violence and sexual assault may behave in ways outsiders consider counterintuitive. Trauma can affect how people organize and describe memories. Disclosure may happen gradually. A victim may cry, appear detached, become angry, laugh nervously, or show little visible emotion. There is no single demeanor that establishes credibility.
Real victims may be frightened, furious, ambivalent, attached to the person harming them, reluctant to involve police, or uncertain about what they want to happen next. They may use substances, have a criminal record, defend themselves, yell back, return to the relationship, or make decisions other people would not make.
Why Leaving Is Not a Single Decision “Just leave” sounds like one action.
In reality, leaving may require many practical resources to line up at once—money, transportation, housing, identification documents, medication, childcare, legal advice, a safe phone, time away from work, a plan for pets, and people who can help without alerting the abusive partner. Much of that preparation may have to happen without the abusive partner noticing.
An abusive person may have spent months or years deliberately dismantling those resources.
Money and housing Financial abuse can leave a victim without savings, credit, bank access, or proof of income. The abusive partner may sabotage employment, run up debt in the victim’s name, hide financial information, or threaten to stop paying for necessities. Even a survivor with an income may not be able to cover deposits, transportation, childcare, legal representation, and replacing essential belongings all at once.
Leaving can also mean risking homelessness. Shelters provide critical support, but they may have limited space or be unable to accommodate every family configuration, disability, pet, work schedule, or safety need. A survivor in a rural area may have few nearby services and no private transportation. Someone in a small community may fear being easily found.
Children and family court Children can be a reason to leave, a reason a victim feels unable to leave, and a tool an abusive partner uses to maintain control.
A survivor may fear that the abusive parent will seek custody, receive unsupervised visitation, refuse to return the children, or use court proceedings to continue harassment. They may fear being accused of parental alienation, violating an existing custody order, or interfering with the other parent’s rights. Some stay because they worry about the children’s safety during visits they will no longer be present for.
The question “Why didn’t they take the children and go?” overlooks how legally complicated—and potentially dangerous—that decision can be.
Isolation and credibility Abuse often weakens the very relationships a victim would need in order to leave. Friends and relatives may have been pushed away. Some may be tired of helping, angry that the victim returned, or convinced the situation cannot be serious because the couple still appears together in public.
The abusive partner may appear calm, generous, or respected outside the home. After living under sustained pressure, the victim may seem anxious, disorganized, angry, or unreliable. That contrast can make the person causing harm look more credible than the person experiencing it.
Love, hope, and responsibility Victims do not necessarily stop loving an abusive partner the moment abuse occurs. They may remember who that person was at the beginning, believe the apologies, hope treatment will work, or want the violence to stop without wanting the relationship to end. Religious beliefs, family expectations, community pressure, and fear of stigma can deepen that conflict.
Abusive partners may alternate cruelty with affection, remorse, gifts, promises, or periods of calm. They may blame stress, alcohol, trauma, jealousy, or the victim. Over time, this creates confusion and hope while reinforcing the idea that peace depends on the victim behaving differently.
Love does not make abuse less serious, but it can help explain why leaving is emotionally complicated.
Disability, discrimination, and dependence Not every survivor faces the same barriers.
A disabled survivor may depend on an abusive partner for personal care, transportation, communication, medication, or assistive devices. An immigrant survivor may fear deportation, language barriers, or losing sponsorship. LGBTQ+ survivors may face threats of being outed, discrimination from services, or disbelief that abuse happens in their relationships. Black, Indigenous, and other survivors of color may weigh the danger at home against experiences of racial bias or the possible consequences of calling law enforcement.
Men can face disbelief, shame, limited services, and cultural expectations that they should be able to stop the abuse themselves. Teenagers may have little privacy, transportation, money, or control over their schedules. Older adults may be financially or medically dependent on the person harming them.
None of these barriers is a personal failing. They are conditions that abuse creates or makes worse.
There is no universal exit plan because there is no universal survivor.
Leaving Can Increase the Danger The most harmful part of “Why didn’t she leave?” is the assumption that leaving ends the abuse.
It may not. For some survivors, the risk increases after separation.
Legal scholar Martha Mahoney named this pattern “separation assault”—violence aimed at preventing a partner from leaving, punishing them for leaving, or forcing them to return.
When a relationship is built on control, leaving directly challenges that control. In response, an abusive person may escalate surveillance, stalking, threats, property damage, legal harassment, abduction, or violence. Abuse can continue through shared children, financial obligations, court proceedings, social media, workplaces, relatives, and new partners.
A landmark multisite case-control study led by Jacquelyn Campbell found that separation from a highly controlling abusive partner was associated with a substantially higher risk of intimate partner femicide. The same research identified other warning signs advocates now use in lethality assessments, including an abuser’s access to a firearm, prior threats with a weapon, and escalating frequency or severity of violence.
Nonfatal strangulation stands out in particular. In one case-control study, women who had previously been strangled by an intimate partner had about 6.7 times the odds of later experiencing attempted homicide and about 7.5 times the odds of becoming victims of completed homicide.
None of this means every survivor who leaves will be killed, or that staying is safe. It means a blanket command to “just leave” can be dangerously incomplete.
Leaving is often a process rather than an event. A survivor may test what is possible, gather documents, hide money, contact an advocate, return when housing falls through, or delay departure until the safest available moment. From the outside, those returns look like indecision. From the inside, they are often safety planning.
That is why advocates don’t simply tell survivors to leave. They help them plan how to leave safely—when to go, where to go, what to take, and what protections may need to be in place. Safety planning respects the survivor as the person with the most detailed knowledge of the abusive partner’s behavior.
An outside observer may want immediate action. A survivor may be weighing risks that are not visible to anyone else.
When a Victim Fights Back Another misconception appears when a victim yells, throws something, strikes back, or otherwise reacts physically.
By the time police arrive, the abusive partner may be calm while the victim is visibly upset. A single snapshot like that can be used to describe the relationship as “mutually abusive,” or to identify the more visibly emotional person as the aggressor.
That conclusion can obscure the larger pattern of abuse.
The phrase “reactive abuse” is commonly used in survivor communities to describe reactions to prolonged mistreatment that may later be used against the victim. Many advocates and researchers prefer terms such as resistive behavior or violent resistance , because labeling a survivor’s response as “abuse” can obscure the larger pattern of coercion and control. Some coercive partners provoke reactions on purpose, then record them, report them, or raise them in custody court.
People experiencing abuse may use force in self-defense, to escape, to protect children, or after a prolonged period of fear and control. That does not mean every act committed by a victim is legally justified, and victimization does not erase accountability for unrelated harm. It does mean that identical acts can carry very different meanings depending on context.
Research supports the distinction. Sociologist Michael Johnson’s typology separates intimate terrorism —violence embedded in a pattern of coercive control—from violent resistance , which is violence used by the person being controlled. Counting incidents without asking who controls the relationship treats these two realities as the same.
The better questions are about the pattern: Who has created fear in the relationship? Who has restricted the other person’s freedom? Who has threatened retaliation? Who is acting to dominate, and who is acting to resist, survive, or get away?
Domestic-violence response guidance increasingly emphasizes identifying the predominant or primary aggressor rather than assuming the person who appears angriest, admits using force, or has caused the most visible injury is necessarily the primary aggressor. A proper assessment looks beyond one moment to the history of violence, coercive control, fear, injuries, threats, self-defense, and each person’s relative ability to cause harm.
This distinction will matter throughout the series. Several of the cases ahead involve victims who were misunderstood, disbelieved, left unprotected, or punished after their behavior was separated from the abuse surrounding it.
Claim vs. Evidence Assessment Claim: “Going back means the victim lied.” Returning can reflect danger, lack of housing, financial dependence, custody concerns, family pressure, or promises of change. It does not show that the original disclosure was false.
Claim: “Both people were toxic, so both were abusive.” Conflict and abuse are not the same thing. Abuse is a pattern of power and control, and one person’s resistance cannot be judged apart from that pattern.
Claim: “A protection order or an arrest solves the problem.” Legal intervention can be essential, but a court order is a tool, not a physical barrier. How much it protects depends on service, enforcement, firearm access, and what the abusive person does next.
The bottom line: The Thurman and Lenahan posts examine what happens when the protection the system promises does not arrive. Change the Question Language shapes where we look for responsibility.
When we ask why a victim stayed, we imply that the survivor’s location caused the abuse. When we ask why they returned, we treat leaving as a test of credibility. When we ask why they did not report sooner, we assume the system was safe and ready to help.
Different questions reveal more of the picture:
What forms of control were present before the physical violence became visible? What did the abusive person threaten to do if the victim left or sought help? What practical resources did the victim actually have? How did police, courts, employers, healthcare providers, schools, or family members respond? What risks did the survivor face by staying—and what different risks by leaving? Who is being held responsible for the abuse? These questions do not remove a survivor’s agency. They recognize that agency can exist under severe constraint. Survivors make choices. But those choices are often made inside conditions another person deliberately created.
How to Support Someone Experiencing Abuse If someone tells you they are being abused, your first response can determine whether they feel safe reaching out again.
Believe them. Avoid demanding proof or criticizing past decisions. Ask what they need rather than taking control. Do not confront the abusive partner or announce a plan without the survivor’s consent—doing so can increase the danger. Offer practical help you can safely and realistically provide, such as storing documents, caring for a pet, providing transportation, or helping them connect with an advocate.
Most importantly, keep the door open. A survivor may not be ready or able to leave when you want them to. Support should not depend on them making the decision you would make.
You can say:
“I believe you. This is not your fault. You do not deserve to be treated this way. I am here to help you think through your options.”
An advocate can help a survivor—or a concerned friend or relative—develop a personalized safety plan. The goal is not to dictate a single course of action. It is to increase safety while respecting the survivor’s knowledge, circumstances, and right to decide what happens next.
If You Need Help Resources National Domestic Violence Hotline: Call 800-799-SAFE (7233), text START to 88788, or chat at TheHotline.org. Free, confidential, and available 24/7.
love is respect (teens and young adults): Call 866-331-9474, text LOVEIS to 22522, or chat at loveisrespect.org.
StrongHearts Native Helpline (Native Americans and Alaska Natives): Call or text 844-7NATIVE (844-762-8483) or visit StrongHeartsHelpline.org. Confidential and available 24/7.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 if it is safe to do so.
Digital safety: Phones, computers, vehicles, shared accounts, and location services can be monitored. If possible, use a device the abusive person cannot access. Clearing your browser history or using private mode does not erase every digital trace. Why This Series Begins Here October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Throughout the month, Crime Central will examine cases that reveal how institutions understand—and misunderstand—abuse.
This series draws on my background in domestic violence advocacy, where I have worked with survivors through safety planning, protection orders, court dates, and the process of leaving. That experience shapes how I approach these cases.
Each Sunday this month, the series will take on one case and one failure point:
The Series October 2026 · Domestic Violence Awareness Month Behind Closed Doors October 1: Beyond “Why Didn’t She Leave?” Coercive control, barriers to leaving, separation violence, and reactive behavior. You are here.
October 4: Tracey Thurman: When Police Treated Domestic Violence as a Private Matter. Police inaction, equal protection, and mandatory-arrest reforms. Coming Sunday.
October 11: Jessica Lenahan: A Protection Order Is Not a Force Field. Protection-order enforcement, police discretion, and state responsibility. Coming October 11.
October 18: Gabby Petito: When Police Mistake the Victim for the Aggressor. Coercive control, reactive behavior, and primary-aggressor identification. Coming October 18.
October 25: Marissa Alexander: When Survivors Are Punished for Fighting Back. Self-defense, race, mandatory minimums, and survivor criminalization. Coming October 25.
The through-line: Each case examines one point where the system meant to protect a victim failed to see the pattern.
These cases are not valuable because they are shocking. They are valuable because each exposes a pattern that extends beyond one household, one police department, or one courtroom.
The blog’s usual editorial standards apply throughout the series. Victims will be treated as people, not plot devices. Evidence will come before narrative, and uncertainty will be named. Violence will be described only as much as understanding requires.
Why It Still Matters The way we ask about abuse shapes what happens next. When a jury treats “Why didn’t she leave?” as the central question, it can decide she must not have been that afraid. When responding officers see only the incident in front of them, they can arrest the wrong person. When a family court sees a parent who keeps going back, it can read instability instead of strategy, and when friends or family ask the same question, the survivor may hear it as blame. Changing the question changes where accountability lands.
Critical Questions Reflection • Inquiry Why these questions: They are meant to carry into the case posts that follow this month.
Should coercive control be specifically criminalized in the United States, as jurisdictions such as England, Wales, and Scotland have done through domestic-abuse legislation? If separation can increase risk, what should police and courts be required to do when a survivor reports that she is leaving? How should officers identify the predominant aggressor in the few minutes they spend at a scene? How do race, immigration status, disability, and gender shape whose account is believed? How can true-crime coverage tell these stories without asking readers to judge the victim’s choices? Editorial note: These prompts are meant to encourage reflection, not to point toward any single conclusion. Final Thoughts Before asking whether a victim behaved the way we think a victim should, we need to understand the conditions under which they were surviving. Before treating leaving as the obvious answer, we need to ask whether the path out was safe, accessible, and supported. Before examining what a survivor did, we need to keep our attention on the person who chose coercion and violence.
The question was never simply why a victim stayed.
The question is how an abusive person built the trap—and what the rest of us did, or failed to do, when the victim tried to escape it.
If You Want to Go Deeper Further Reading Coercive Control: How Men Entrap Women in Personal Life Evan Stark · 2007 · Book The book that framed abuse as a crime against liberty rather than a series of separate assaults.
Legal Images of Battered Women: Redefining the Issue of Separation Martha Mahoney · 1991 · Law review article The article that named “separation assault” and questioned the law’s focus on why women stay.
Risk Factors for Femicide in Abusive Relationships Campbell et al. · 2003 · Peer-reviewed study The multisite study behind modern lethality assessment, including the risk tied to separation from a controlling partner.
Non-Fatal Strangulation Is an Important Risk Factor for Homicide of Women Glass et al. · 2008 · Peer-reviewed study The source of the attempted- and completed-homicide odds cited in this post.
A Typology of Domestic Violence Michael P. Johnson · 2008 · Book Distinguishes intimate terrorism from violent resistance, background for the Petito and Alexander posts.
National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey: 2023/2024 Data Brief Centers for Disease Control and Prevention · 2026 · Primary source The national prevalence figures used in this post, including the survey’s measures of coercive control.
